A postponement is the act of moving something from its original, planned time to a later time — intentionally, by someone's decision.

Think of it this way: something was supposed to happen at a specific time, but instead of happening then, it gets pushed forward in time. It will still happen — just later than originally planned.

Simple example: Your dentist appointment was on Monday at 10 AM. On Sunday night, the dentist calls and says she can't see you Monday — can you come on Thursday instead? That shift from Monday to Thursday is a postponement.
The Three Things That Must Be True

For something to be a postponement, three conditions must be present:

  1. Something was already planned. There was a specific time or date set for an event, meeting, task, or decision.
  2. It was deliberately moved back in time. Someone — a person, an organization, an authority — made the conscious decision to delay it.
  3. It will still happen — just later. It has not been abandoned or cancelled.

If any of these three are missing, it's not quite a postponement. For example, if your train is late because of heavy rain, that's a delay — not a postponement, because no one decided to push it back. And if your dentist cancels your appointment permanently with no rescheduling, that's a cancellation, not a postponement.
The Most Important Distinction: Postponement vs. Cancellation

This is the sharpest, most critical line to understand.

  • A postponement = "This will still happen, but at a different, later time."
  • A cancellation = "This will NOT happen at all."

When the Tokyo Olympics were moved from 2020 to 2021 due to the pandemic, that was a postponement — the games were delayed, but they still took place.

If the games had been called off entirely and never held, that would have been a cancellation.

This distinction matters a lot in real life. When someone hears "the concert is postponed," they know to keep their tickets — it's still coming. When they hear "the concert is cancelled," they ask for a refund.
The New Date: Known or Unknown?

A postponement doesn't always come with a new date immediately. There are two kinds:

  • Postponement with a new date: "The meeting has been postponed to November 15th." Here you know exactly when it will happen.
  • Open-ended postponement: "The trial has been postponed until further notice." Here it is confirmed that it will still happen, but the new date hasn't been decided yet.

Both are postponements. The second kind is sometimes called an indefinite postponement, meaning there's no clear timeline for when it will eventually occur.
What Postponement Implies About Intent

A postponement is always a deliberate act. When something is postponed, somebody chose to delay it. It might be because:

  • Circumstances changed (bad weather, illness, conflict)
  • More preparation is needed
  • Key people cannot attend
  • Resources aren't ready
  • External factors (like a government order) force the delay

Whatever the reason, the word "postponement" always carries the idea that someone made this call. It is not an accident; it is a decision.
How It's Used in Real Life — Contexts

Postponement appears across almost every area of life. Here are some common contexts where you'll encounter the word:

  • Events: A sports match, concert, wedding ceremony, or awards show can be postponed.
  • Meetings and sessions: A business meeting, a court hearing, a parliament session, or a school exam can be postponed.
  • Decisions: A judge might announce the postponement of a verdict. A company might announce the postponement of a decision on hiring.
  • Projects and launches: A rocket launch, a product release, or a construction project can face postponement.
  • Medical: A surgery or a medical procedure can be postponed.
  • Legal and official: Elections, trials, and policy implementations can be postponed.
Common Phrases and Collocations

In natural English, "postponement" appears frequently in these patterns:

  • "the postponement of [something]" → "the postponement of the elections," "the postponement of the meeting"
  • "announce a postponement" → to make the delay known publicly
  • "request a postponement" → to formally ask for more time before something happens
  • "grant a postponement" → to officially allow a delay that was requested
  • "due to the postponement" → explaining what happened as a result of the delay
  • "indefinite postponement" → a delay with no fixed new date
  • "repeated postponement" → when something is delayed again and again
The Noun in Action — Examples

To really cement the meaning, here are clear example sentences:

  1. The postponement of the cricket match disappointed thousands of fans who had already bought tickets.

(The match was moved to a later date; it wasn't cancelled.)

  1. She welcomed the postponement of her exam because she needed more time to study.

(The exam date was pushed forward; it will still happen later.)

  1. The court announced a postponement of the trial until January due to the judge's illness.

(The trial is delayed, not abandoned.)

  1. After three postponements, people started to wonder if the project would ever be completed.

(It had been delayed three times in a row — still not cancelled, but very delayed.)

  1. The indefinite postponement of the summit left world leaders uncertain about when they would meet.

(Delayed with no new date fixed yet.)
Repeated Postponements — An Important Real-World Note

Sometimes, something gets postponed not once but multiple times. Each delay is a separate postponement. Over time, repeated postponements can start to feel like a quiet cancellation — because even though the event is never officially called off, it never seems to actually happen either.

This is why "indefinite postponement" can sometimes be a polite or cautious way of saying something might not happen at all. Politicians, for instance, sometimes postpone controversial decisions again and again without ever cancelling them outright.
How It Relates to Similar Words

Understanding how "postponement" compares to near-synonyms helps sharpen your grasp of it:

  • Delay is broader and more general. A delay can be accidental (a traffic jam caused a delay) or intentional. Postponement is always intentional. Also, "postponement" is more formal.
  • Deferral is very close in meaning. It tends to appear in formal, legal, financial, or official contexts — "deferral of payment," "deferral of a decision." It's a slightly more technical word than postponement.
  • Adjournment specifically means the postponement of a formal session — like a court case, a parliament sitting, or a board meeting. When a judge says "court is adjourned," it means the proceedings are being paused and will resume later.
  • Rescheduling simply means setting a new time. It can mean moving something earlier OR later. Postponement specifically means moving it later.
  • Putting off or putting something on hold are informal, everyday expressions for the same idea as postponement.
The Word as a "Count" Noun

"Postponement" is a count noun, meaning you can talk about one postponement, two postponements, etc. You can refer to:

  • A single act of postponing: "The postponement was announced at noon."
  • Multiple instances: "There have been three postponements so far this year."
Summary in One Sentence
A postponement is a deliberate decision to move something from its planned time to a later time, with the understanding that it will still happen — just not when originally intended.
